Eight ways to learn a pattern

Tree methods ask questions. Splines assemble bends. Ensembles combine learners. SVMs optimize a separating margin. Keep the task, objective and regularization separate when explaining any algorithm.

A short review route
  1. Read the exam essentials and say the objective aloud.
  2. Step through the numerical example before opening the mathematics.
  3. Answer five recall prompts from memory, then reveal each explanation.
  4. Tick only the skills you can reproduce without looking.

This guide contains eight lessons and 40 ungraded recall prompts. Your optional responses, reveals, ticks and walkthrough positions last only while the document is open. Reopening starts fresh. Nothing is saved or submitted.

FamilyAlgorithmsMain question
Single treeID3, C4.5, CART, CHAIDWhich split should this node make?
SplineMARSWhich hinge terms describe the response?
EnsembleRandom Forest, Gradient BoostingHow should multiple learners combine?
MarginSVM / SVRWhich regularized boundary or regression tube fits?

Only gradient boosting here has a boosting-style learning rate. “No learning rate” for the other algorithms does not imply their training is noniterative. Hyperparameters still control complexity, statistics or numerical optimization.

LESSON 01 / 08 · SINGLE TREE

ID3

Iterative Dichotomiser 3

Ross Quinlan · 1986

ClassificationInformation gain

Exam essentials

  • Choose the attribute with the largest reduction in weighted class entropy.
  • Classic ID3 branches on categorical values. It does not search numeric thresholds natively.
  • A pure node has entropy 0; a balanced binary node has entropy 1 bit. For C classes the maximum is log₂(C).

Intuition

Ask the question that removes the most uncertainty about the class. A good question creates children whose class mixes are more certain than the parent. Weight each child by its size: a tiny pure leaf should not count as much as a large mixed leaf.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
H(S) = −Σᵢ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ), with 0 log₂(0) = 0
I(A) = Σᵥ (nᵥ/n) H(Sᵥ) ··· Gain(S,A) = H(S) − I(A)

Here pᵢ is the proportion of class i at the current node; Sᵥ contains rows with A = v. Information gain is measured in bits. The parent is fixed while candidates are compared.

Complexity control: Stop when pure, no useful attributes remain, or a stopping rule is met; original ID3 has no post-pruning.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

# Generate synthetic discrete multi-class classification data
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randint(0, 3, size=(100, 2))  # Discrete categorical feature matrix
y = ((X[:, 0] == 1) & (X[:, 1] != 0)).astype(int)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
depths = [1, 3, None]

for ax, depth in zip(axes, depths):
    # Entropy-based CART demonstration (not categorical ID3)
    clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', max_depth=depth, random_state=42)
    clf.fit(X, y)
    
    plot_tree(clf, ax=ax, feature_names=['Feature_A', 'Feature_B'], 
              class_names=['No', 'Yes'], filled=True, rounded=True)
    ax.set_title(f"Entropy-based CART (max_depth={depth})")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Correction noteThe source’s entropy-based scikit-learn script is retained below with an accurate CART label. Integer category codes introduce an order; genuine categorical ID3 uses a branch per value. More depth can fit more detail, but purity and overfitting are not guaranteed.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • High entropy is uncertainty, not a good split score. Maximize gain, not child entropy.
  • An identifier can create one pure child per row and obtain the full parent entropy as gain. This is high-arity bias, not evidence of useful prediction.
  • Splitting is recursive, not a single pass. Contradictory labels for identical features or exhausted attributes can leave impure leaves.
  • A finite training set has finitely many observed numerical values. The issue with numeric data is the lack of a native threshold-search rule, not infinitely many observed rows.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Entropy of 8 positive and 0 negative examples?

Reveal answer 1

0 bits. The node is pure; use the convention 0 log₂(0)=0.

2. Parent entropy 0.940; weighted child entropy 0.788. What is the gain?

Reveal answer 2

Using these rounded inputs: 0.940 − 0.788 = 0.152 bits.

3. Why does classic ID3 need adaptation for continuous predictors?

Reveal answer 3

Its native rule creates branches for categorical values; it has no numerical threshold search. Discretize or use an extension. A finite dataset does not contain infinitely many observed values.

4. Entropy of 5 positive and 5 negative examples?

Reveal answer 4

1 bit: −2(0.5 log₂ 0.5). This is the binary maximum.

5. When is information gain exactly zero?

Reveal answer 5

When weighted child entropy equals parent entropy; for a nonempty deterministic partition, every positive-weight child has the same class distribution as the parent.

← OverviewC4.5 →

LESSON 02 / 08 · SINGLE TREE

C4.5

Gain ratio and numerical thresholds

Ross Quinlan · 1993

ClassificationGain ratio

Exam essentials

  • C4.5 is a classification algorithm; continuous predictors do not make its target a regression target.
  • Normalize information gain by split information and screen out unhelpfully low-gain splits.
  • Sort numerical values and consider adjacent midpoints; the same numeric predictor can appear again down a path.

Intuition

Information gain can reward a question just for offering many answers. Gain ratio discounts the information used to identify the branch. Then pruning asks whether keeping a subtree is justified by estimated prediction error.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
SplitInfo(A) = −Σᵥ (nᵥ/n) log₂(nᵥ/n)
GainRatio(A) = Gain(S,A) / SplitInfo(A)
Candidate midpoint tᵢ = (xᵢ + xᵢ₊₁)/2

Split information depends on branch sizes, not class labels. Do not divide by zero for a constant attribute. A small denominator can favor an unbalanced low-gain split, so C4.5 uses a gain screen. The table teaches midpoint comparison; full C4.5 also includes implementation-specific threshold selection and corrections.

Complexity control: Error-based post-pruning; gain-ratio selection reduces high-arity preference but does not eliminate overfitting.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# Generate synthetic non-linear continuous dataset
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randn(150, 2)
y = (X[:, 0]**2 + X[:, 1]**2 > 1.2).astype(int)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Unpruned Tree (Vulnerable to noise memorization in a CART model)
clf_unpruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', random_state=42)
clf_unpruned.fit(X, y)

# CART Cost-Complexity Pruning (not C4.5 error-based pruning) (ccp_alpha)
clf_pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', ccp_alpha=0.03, random_state=42)
clf_pruned.fit(X, y)

# Render Decision Boundaries
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 200), np.linspace(-3, 3, 200))
for ax, model, title in zip(axes, [clf_unpruned, clf_pruned], 
                            ["Unpruned Decision Boundary", "Pruned (ccp_alpha=0.03) Boundary"]):
    Z = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap='coolwarm')
    ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y, cmap='coolwarm', edgecolors='k')
    ax.set_title(title)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Correction noteThe original pruning demo is retained as an entropy-based CART comparison. A simpler boundary is visible on this dataset; better unseen accuracy requires validation. C4.5 can also handle missing predictors through weighted treatment, beyond this complete-data example.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • Gain ratio reduces, rather than abolishes, high-arity bias. It is not simply “always pick the largest ratio” without safeguards.
  • Continuous predictors are supported; C4.5 itself is not a general regression-tree algorithm.
  • Pre-pruning stops growth early. Post-pruning simplifies a tree after growth.
  • C4.5’s error-based pruning differs from CART’s cost-complexity pruning. ccp_alpha is not a C4.5 parameter.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Define gain ratio and its components.

Reveal answer 1

GainRatio = Gain / SplitInfo, where Gain = H(parent) − weighted H(children) and SplitInfo = −Σᵥ(nᵥ/n)log₂(nᵥ/n). A zero denominator is not an eligible split.

2. How does C4.5 reduce high-arity feature bias?

Reveal answer 2

It normalizes information gain by branch-size entropy, with a gain-based eligibility screen. This reduces the preference; it does not eliminate all bias.

3. True or false: a numeric predictor can be split only once along a C4.5 path.

Reveal answer 3

False. It can be tested again at different thresholds.

4. How are continuous threshold candidates evaluated?

Reveal answer 4

Sort distinct values, consider adjacent midpoints and compare binary partitions using entropy-based selection. The simplified example compares gain ratios; full C4.5 has additional threshold-selection rules.

5. How does C4.5 control an overly complex tree?

Reveal answer 5

It uses error-based post-pruning after growth. Do not equate this with CART cost-complexity pruning.

LESSON 03 / 08 · SINGLE TREE

CART

Classification and Regression Trees

Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone · 1984

Classification & regressionGini / squared error

Exam essentials

  • Every internal CART split has two children.
  • For classification minimize weighted Gini; for squared-error regression minimize weighted within-child MSE.
  • Squared-error leaves predict their target mean. Ordinary regression-tree predictions are piecewise constant.

Intuition

Try a yes/no question and measure how much more alike the outcomes become within each group. In regression, replacing one global mean with two local means can sharply reduce squared error.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
G(S) = 1 − Σᵢ pᵢ² ··· Gsplit = (nL/n) GL + (nR/n) GR
MSEK = (1/nK) Σᵢ∈K (yᵢ − ȳK)²
MSEsplit = (nL/n) MSEL + (nR/n) MSER

Parent impurity is constant across candidate splits. Therefore maximizing parent − weighted children is exactly equivalent to minimizing weighted children. Binary Gini is at most 0.5; with C equally frequent classes it is 1 − 1/C. Gini equals the probability that two independent draws from the node’s class distribution disagree, not the error of the majority-class predictor.

Cost-complexity objective: Rα(T) = R(T) + α · number_of_leaves(T)

For m unordered predictor categories, there are (2ᵐ − 2)/2 = 2ᵐ⁻¹ − 1 distinct nonempty binary partitions, counting a partition and its complement once. Implementations can use shortcuts. scikit-learn trees require numeric encoding; integer labels alone do not implement unrestricted subset search.

Complexity control: Depth and leaf-size constraints or minimal cost-complexity post-pruning.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

# Generate non-linear continuous regression target data
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.sort(5 * np.random.rand(80, 1), axis=0)
y = np.sin(X).ravel() + np.random.normal(0, 0.1, X.shape[0])

# Fit Regression Trees with varying depth limits
regr_shallow = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=42)
regr_deep = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=6, random_state=42)
regr_shallow.fit(X, y)
regr_deep.fit(X, y)

X_test = np.arange(0.0, 5.0, 0.01)[:, np.newaxis]
y_shallow = regr_shallow.predict(X_test)
y_deep = regr_deep.predict(X_test)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(X, y, s=20, edgecolor="black", c="darkorange", label="Data Points")
plt.plot(X_test, y_shallow, color="cornflowerblue", label="max_depth=2 (Step Approx)", linewidth=2)
plt.plot(X_test, y_deep, color="crimson", label="max_depth=6 (More detail)", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Input Feature (X)")
plt.ylabel("Target Value (Y)")
plt.title("CART Regression Step-Function Fits Under Structural Depth Constraints")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
Correction noteHouse prices use $k consistently: [100,120,140,300,320]. Dividing by $10k gives [10,12,14,30,32]. The mean is 196 (not the source?s 176). Correct reduction is 8664/8864 ≈ 97.74%, not 99.17%. The latter percentage belongs to the separate [10,12,14,50,54] series.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • The source’s [10,12,14,50,54] is a separate target series, not the house prices divided by $10,000.
  • Scaling every target by a multiplies MSE by a². The unregularized split ranking is unchanged; fixed impurity thresholds or ccp_alpha may need rescaling.
  • Deep trees can overfit, but zero impurity is impossible with some conflicting data. max_depth=2 gives at most four leaves, not exactly four.
  • Gini and entropy can choose different splits. The source’s “over 90%” agreement and guaranteed calibration claim have no supporting evidence.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Gini impurity of 6 positive and 4 negative examples?

Reveal answer 1

1 − (0.6² + 0.4²) = 0.48.

2. Why does minimizing weighted child Gini maximize Gini gain?

Reveal answer 2

Gain = parent Gini − weighted child Gini. The parent is the same constant for all candidates at this node.

3. Write weighted MSE and define its terms.

Reveal answer 3

(nL/n)MSEL + (nR/n)MSER, where each MSE is the average squared deviation from that child’s mean and n=nL+nR.

4. Maximum possible binary Gini impurity?

Reveal answer 4

0.5, attained at class proportions 0.5 and 0.5.

5. How many binary partitions exist for m unordered predictor categories?

Reveal answer 5

2^(m−1) − 1 distinct nonempty partitions, ignoring left/right duplicates. Practical CART implementations can use shortcuts; scikit-learn does not natively enumerate categorical subset splits.

← C4.5CHAID →

LESSON 04 / 08 · SINGLE TREE

CHAID

Chi-square Automatic Interaction Detection

Gordon Kass · 1980

Classification & regressionAdjusted significance tests

Exam essentials

  • Categorical-target CHAID uses association tests on contingency tables.
  • Merge categories with similar target distributions, then compare eligible predictors using adjusted p-values.
  • A nonsignificant candidate is rejected; the node stops only if no candidate qualifies or another stopping rule is met.

Intuition

Group predictor categories that behave alike, then ask whether the remaining groups differ enough in their outcomes to justify branches. A tiny p-value is evidence against independence under the test assumptions, not an accuracy score or proof of causality.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
Eᵢⱼ = (row_totalᵢ × column_totalⱼ) / N
χ² = Σᵢ Σⱼ (Oᵢⱼ − Eᵢⱼ)² / Eᵢⱼ ··· df = (r−1)(c−1)

O is observed frequency; E is expected frequency under independence. Counts must be nonnegative and observations independent; sparse expected cells can invalidate the asymptotic approximation. Multiple comparisons call for adjusted significance. For continuous targets, CHAID extensions use an F test rather than a class contingency test. Continuous predictors are typically binned before category merging.

Complexity control: Merge statistically similar categories; split only when a candidate meets the adjusted significance and size rules.

Python output and interpretation
χ² = 36.0; p ≈ 1.973175290e-09; df = 1; expected cells = 25

correction=False reproduces the hand calculation. The default correction gives χ²=33.64. Neither single test implements the complete CHAID search.

Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Synthetic Contingency Matrix simulating CHAID node evaluation
np.random.seed(42)
observed_data = np.array([[40, 10], [10, 40]])  # Segment vs Renewal

chi2_stat, p_val, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(observed_data, correction=False)

print(f"Pearson node-test demo (not full CHAID):")
print(f"Calculated Chi2 Statistic: {chi2_stat:.4f}")
print(f"p-value: {p_val:.8e}")
print(f"Degrees of Freedom: {dof}")
if p_val < 0.05:
    print("Decision: Reject Null Hypothesis -> Candidate significant; full CHAID also merges and adjusts tests.")
else:
    print("Decision: Do not reject independence; test other eligible candidates.")
Correction noteThe worked calculation explicitly uses uncorrected Pearson χ². The category-merging extension is labeled illustrative and is distinct from the original 100-customer table. α=0.05 is a chosen setting, not a universal constant.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • A 2×2 example produces two branches; multiway-capable does not mean every split has three or more children.
  • Failing to reject independence does not prove independence.
  • SciPy’s default Yates correction at df=1 gives 33.64 here. Use correction=False to match the hand Pearson statistic of 36.
  • One chi-square test is a node-evaluation demonstration, not a full CHAID implementation with category merging and multiplicity adjustment.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Which test does categorical-target CHAID use?

Reveal answer 1

A chi-square association test (Pearson or likelihood-ratio variant depending on settings), together with category merging and adjusted significance. Continuous-target variants use F tests.

2. Expected frequency for cell (i,j)?

Reveal answer 2

Eᵢⱼ = row_totalᵢ × column_totalⱼ / grand_total.

3. How does CHAID branching differ from CART?

Reveal answer 3

CHAID can create multiple branches after category merging; CART creates exactly two children per split. CHAID can also produce a two-branch split.

4. A candidate’s adjusted p-value exceeds α=0.05. What stops?

Reveal answer 4

That candidate is not selected. The whole node becomes terminal only if no other eligible predictor meets the split and size rules. Failing to reject is not proof of independence.

5. Why use CHAID for categorical survey data?

Reveal answer 5

It can group categories with similar target distributions and produce interpretable multiway segments, subject to sample-size and test assumptions.

← CARTMARS →

LESSON 05 / 08 · SPLINE

MARS

Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines

Jerome Friedman · 1991

RegressionHinge basis functions

Exam essentials

  • A hinge changes slope at a knot while staying continuous.
  • Fit a linear combination of basis functions; products can represent interactions.
  • Adaptive knot/basis selection distinguishes MARS from fitting a preselected spline basis.

Intuition

Build a curve from bendable rulers. Each hinge starts contributing on one side of its knot. Coefficients control slopes; adding hinges provides flexibility, and deleting weak terms limits unnecessary complexity.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
b⁺(x) = max(0,x−c) ··· b⁻(x) = max(0,c−x)
f(x) = β₀ + Σₘ βₘ Bₘ(x)
GCV ≈ (RSS/n) / (1 − Ceff/n)²

c is a knot; Bₘ is a hinge or product of hinges; coefficients β are fitted by least squares for a chosen basis. Forward selection tries candidate hinge pairs (possibly multiplying an existing basis) for error reduction. Backward deletion creates smaller models; a criterion such as GCV balances fit and effective complexity Ceff. Constraints limit basis count and interaction degree.

Complexity control: Forward basis expansion followed by backward deletion and complexity-adjusted model selection.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Generate smooth non-linear continuous target data
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y = np.sin(x) + 0.1 * x + np.random.normal(0, 0.1, 100)

# Fixed-knot hinge basis demo; does not perform adaptive MARS selection
def hinge_right(x, c): return np.maximum(0, x - c)
def hinge_left(x, c):  return np.maximum(0, c - x)

# Build synthetic MARS basis matrix with knots at x=3.0 and x=7.0
X_basis = np.column_stack([
    np.ones_like(x),
    hinge_left(x, 3.0),
    hinge_right(x, 3.0),
    hinge_right(x, 7.0)
])

# Solve coefficients analytically via least squares
coeffs, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(X_basis, y, rcond=None)
y_pred = X_basis @ coeffs

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.6, label="Sample Observations")
plt.plot(x, y_pred, color="red", linewidth=2.5, label="Fixed-knot hinge spline fit")
plt.axvline(3.0, linestyle="--", color="gray", label="Knot 1 (c=3.0)")
plt.axvline(7.0, linestyle="--", color="black", label="Knot 2 (c=7.0)")
plt.xlabel("Continuous Predictor (X)")
plt.ylabel("Target Value (Y)")
plt.title("Fixed-knot spline: least-squares fit across two knots")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
Correction noteThe source script is retained and relabeled “fixed-knot hinge spline.” The walkthrough separately explains adaptive forward/backward construction. Ordinary MARS fitting has no boosting-style learning-rate parameter.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • A hinge spline is continuous, but its derivative can jump at a knot. “Continuous” does not mean smooth to every derivative order.
  • A forward pass builds a flexible model that may overfit; overfitting is not guaranteed at every forward step.
  • Fixed knots at 3 and 7 plus least squares demonstrate the basis algebra, not full adaptive MARS.
  • Local hinges avoid one global high-degree polynomial, but do not guarantee stable extrapolation or superiority on every dataset.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Define the complementary hinges at knot c.

Reveal answer 1

b⁺(x)=max(0,x−c) and b⁻(x)=max(0,c−x). Both are zero at x=c.

2. How does a MARS fit differ from a CART regression fit?

Reveal answer 2

Ordinary CART has piecewise constant leaves; first-order MARS combines continuous piecewise linear hinges. Hinges can have slope discontinuities.

3. What happens in the MARS forward pass?

Reveal answer 3

Candidate hinge pairs and interactions are added to improve fit, refitting coefficients. The growing model is flexible and can overfit; this is not guaranteed at every step.

4. Which criterion selects among pruned MARS models?

Reveal answer 4

Typically generalized cross-validation (GCV), balancing residual error against effective complexity. Validation can also guide model selection.

5. True or false: ordinary MARS requires gradient descent to fit coefficients.

Reveal answer 5

False. For a chosen basis the coefficients are estimated by least squares, usually with numerical linear algebra. Basis selection is a separate adaptive process.

LESSON 06 / 08 · ENSEMBLE

Random Forest

Bootstrap aggregation with random features

Breiman · 2001; related random-subspace work: Ho · 1995

Classification & regressionBagging + feature randomness

Exam essentials

  • With bootstrap=True, draw n training rows with replacement for each tree.
  • Choose candidate features again at each node, rather than once for a whole tree.
  • OOB prediction for a row uses only trees whose bootstrap samples omitted that row.

Intuition

Ask a committee whose members saw different resampled data and different candidate questions. Averaging reduces the influence of individual trees when their errors are not perfectly correlated. Trees can be trained independently conditional on the data, though their predictions remain correlated.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
P(row omitted) = (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.3679
Regression: ŷ(x) = (1/B) Σᵦ fᵦ(x)
Hard vote: ŷ(x) = argmaxc Σᵦ 1[fᵦ(x)=c]

The hard-vote formula is the pedagogical example below. scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier averages tree class probabilities and chooses the largest average, which can differ from voting on hard labels. With fully pure leaves these often coincide. For equally variable trees, ensemble variance is approximately ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B: correlation ρ sets a floor.

With 16 predictors and max_features="sqrt", K=4. P/3 is a historical regression heuristic, not the current scikit-learn RandomForestRegressor default (1.0, all features). n_jobs=-1 requests all available processors, subject to the runtime. criterion applies to tree split quality; regression criteria differ from classification criteria.

Complexity control: Average decorrelated trees; tune tree constraints and feature randomness using validation.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

# Generate multi-feature synthetic classification dataset
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=500, n_features=10, n_informative=5, random_state=42)

estimator_counts = [1, 5, 50, 200]
oob_scores = []

for n in estimator_counts:
    clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n, oob_score=True, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
    clf.fit(X, y)
    oob_scores.append(clf.oob_score_ if n > 1 else np.nan)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(estimator_counts[1:], oob_scores[1:], marker='o', linewidth=2, color='green')
plt.xlabel("Number of Trees (n_estimators)")
plt.ylabel("Out-of-Bag (OOB) Validation Score")
plt.title("Seeded OOB scores (not guaranteed monotonic)")
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
Correction noteThe OOB plot is generated from the retained seeded script. Small forests can leave rows without OOB predictions and issue a warning. Increasing B addresses Monte Carlo variation, not every source of bias or overfitting.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • 36.8% is a large-n expected omission fraction for n draws, not an exact fraction in every bootstrap sample.
  • A row included even once in a tree’s training sample is not OOB for that tree.
  • More trees often stabilize predictions; validation/OOB scores need not rise monotonically and do not provide immunity to overfitting.
  • A large training–OOB gap suggests generalization problems. Similar scores alone do not establish good performance; compare to a baseline and use leakage-safe evaluation.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. With P=16 and max_features="sqrt", how many candidate features per node?

Reveal answer 1

K=4. This explicitly states the scikit-learn classifier default setting; other settings can differ.

2. What fraction of rows are OOB for one n-draw bootstrap sample?

Reveal answer 2

The expected fraction is (1−1/n)^n, tending to e^−1 ≈ 36.8% for large n. Actual membership varies by tree.

3. Contrast bagging with boosting.

Reveal answer 3

Bagging aggregates independently constructed resampled learners and often reduces variance. Boosting adds learners sequentially to loss gradients and can reduce bias; either method also affects other error components.

4. What does n_jobs=-1 request in RandomForestClassifier?

Reveal answer 4

All available processors for supported parallel operations over trees, subject to the execution environment.

5. Does increasing tree count from 200 to 2000 necessarily cause overfitting?

Reveal answer 5

No. More trees usually stabilize the ensemble. But validation scores need not improve monotonically, and forests can still overfit or be mis-evaluated.

Revision checklist

Course: RANDOM FOREST -oob_score.pdf, pp. 1–2; Ensemble of Trees - Notes.pdf, pp. 1–8. Reference [6].

← MARSGradient Boosting →

LESSON 07 / 08 · ENSEMBLE

Gradient Boosting

Sequential fitting to loss gradients

Jerome Friedman · 2001 (1999 technical report)

Classification & regressionNegative loss gradients

Exam essentials

  • Fit a new learner to pseudo-residuals of the current model.
  • For half squared-error loss, pseudo-residuals are y − F(x); other losses have different gradients.
  • learning_rate scales each new contribution and must be tuned together with n_estimators.

Intuition

Start with a simple prediction, then ask each new small tree to repair the remaining pattern of error. Each tree sees the consequences of the earlier ones, so stage order matters.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
F₀ = argminc Σᵢ L(yᵢ,c)
rᵢₘ = −[∂L(yᵢ,F(xᵢ))/∂F(xᵢ)] at F=Fₘ₋₁
Fₘ(x) = Fₘ₋₁(x) + η γₘ hₘ(x)

For squared error, F₀ is the training-target mean. hₘ approximates the negative gradient; γₘ or leaf-specific updates minimize loss along the new direction. The walkthrough absorbs that factor into hₘ. For classification the model commonly operates on raw scores, not directly on class labels or probabilities.

Complexity control: Shrinkage, shallow trees, subsampling and validation-based early stopping.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

# Generate continuous regression target dataset
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.linspace(0, 10, 200).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.sin(X).ravel() + np.random.normal(0, 0.15, 200)

learning_rates = [0.01, 0.1, 1.0]
iterations = 100
sample_idx = 50  # Fixed observation point for tracking

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

for lr in learning_rates:
    gbm = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=iterations, learning_rate=lr, max_depth=2, random_state=42)
    gbm.fit(X, y)
    
    # Extract stagewise cumulative predictions for the selected sample
    staged_preds = [p[0] for p in gbm.staged_predict(X[sample_idx].reshape(1, -1))]
    plt.plot(range(1, iterations + 1), staged_preds, label=f"learning_rate (eta) = {lr}")

plt.axhline(y[sample_idx], linestyle="--", color="black", label="True Target Value")
plt.xlabel("Boosting Iterations (m)")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Prediction F_m(x)")
plt.title("Impact of Learning Rate (eta) on GBM Trajectory Convergence")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
Correction noteThe three source weak-learner outputs are illustrative, not trees fitted to a one-row dataset. Learning-rate comparisons below are actual independently refitted models; changing η changes later residuals and trees.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • Weak learners fit pseudo-residuals, not the original target afresh each time.
  • A supplied F₀=70 can be the mean of a larger training set; it is not the mean of the single illustrated y=100.
  • η=1 does not necessarily oscillate or overshoot. Inspect generated results; a single point’s fit is not a generalization test.
  • Lower η often needs more stages but does not guarantee better validation error. Boosting can affect both bias and variance, not only bias.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. Write the stagewise GBM update.

Reveal answer 1

Fₘ=Fₘ₋₁+ηγₘhₘ. η is shrinkage, hₘ is the new learner and γₘ is a loss-minimizing step factor (or included in leaf updates).

2. What target does the new weak learner fit?

Reveal answer 2

Pseudo-residuals: the negative gradient of loss with respect to the current prediction. For half squared error these are y−Fₘ₋₁(x).

3. What is the learning-rate / estimator-count tradeoff?

Reveal answer 3

Smaller learning rates generally need more stages for comparable training fit and can improve validation performance when tuned. They do not guarantee better generalization.

4. What are the usual motivations for bagging and boosting?

Reveal answer 4

Bagging often reduces variance by averaging decorrelated learners; boosting often reduces bias by sequential corrections. These are tendencies, not exclusive effects.

5. Must η=1 cause overshoot and oscillation?

Reveal answer 5

No. It uses an unshrunk update and can fit rapidly; instability or overfitting depends on the data, loss, tree size and stage count. Inspect curves and validation error.

Revision checklist

Course: Gradient Boosting.pdf, pp. 1–6; Gradient Boosting Model - Prediction.pdf, pp. 1–2; GB Machines - learning_rate.pdf, pp. 1–2. Reference [6].

← Random ForestSVM →

LESSON 08 / 08 · MARGIN

SVM

Support Vector Machine

Boser, Guyon & Vapnik · 1992; Cortes & Vapnik · 1995

Classification & regressionRegularized maximum margin

Exam essentials

  • The boundary is wᵀx+b=0; w is perpendicular to it.
  • In canonical hard-margin scaling, the two supporting planes are wᵀx+b=±1.
  • Kernels compute inner products in a feature space, giving nonlinear input-space boundaries without explicit coordinates.

Intuition

Place a separating ruler between classes with as much clearance as possible. When perfect separation is unreasonable, allow penalized margin violations. Only samples with nonzero dual coefficients contribute to the prediction expansion.

Guided example

Mathematics and deeper explanation
Distance to boundary = |wᵀx+b| / ‖w‖
One-sided canonical margin = 1/‖w‖ ··· full width = 2/‖w‖
Hard margin: minimize ½‖w‖² subject to yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ+b) ≥ 1
Soft margin: minimize ½‖w‖² + CΣᵢ ξᵢ; yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ+b) ≥ 1−ξᵢ; ξᵢ ≥ 0
Linear: K(x,z)=xᵀz ··· RBF: exp(−γ‖x−z‖²)
Polynomial: K(x,z)=(γxᵀz+r)ᵈ

Larger C penalizes margin violations more strongly, weakening regularization; lower C permits more violation. These are tradeoffs, not guaranteed changes in test error or every local boundary. γ controls RBF locality and also enters the polynomial kernel. Standardization is usually important for distance-based kernels; fit scaling only on training folds, typically in a pipeline. SVR is the regression variant with an ε-insensitive tube.

Complexity control: Soft-margin penalty C, kernel capacity and validation with correctly fitted scaling.

Generated Python result and interpretation
Corrected Python visualization script

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Generate non-linearly separable dataset
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randn(100, 2)
y = np.where(X[:, 0]**2 + X[:, 1]**2 > 1.0, 1, -1)

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)  # demonstration; fit scaler inside CV for evaluation
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Soft Margin SVM (C=0.1, RBF Kernel)
svm_soft = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=0.1, gamma='scale', random_state=42)
svm_soft.fit(X, y)

# Less regularized soft-margin SVM (C=100.0, RBF Kernel)
svm_high_c = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=100.0, gamma='scale', random_state=42)
svm_high_c.fit(X, y)

xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 200), np.linspace(-3, 3, 200))

for ax, model, title in zip(axes, [svm_soft, svm_high_c], 
                            ["Soft margin, C=0.1", "Soft margin, C=100"]):
    Z = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
    ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap='bwr')
    ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y, cmap='bwr', edgecolors='k')
    # Highlight identified support vectors
    ax.scatter(model.support_vectors_[:, 0], model.support_vectors_[:, 1],
               s=100, facecolors='none', edgecolors='k', linewidths=1.5, label="Support Vectors")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Generated kernel / C comparison gallery

Blue: +1; orange: −1; outlined points: solver support vectors. Same 100 rows and scaling in every panel; polynomial degree=3, coef0=1, gamma="scale".

Compare shapes and support-vector counts; these training fits do not establish a winning model. For unbiased assessment, put StandardScaler inside a cross-validated pipeline.

Python code for the extended kernel / C gallery

Run in Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib installed. Code is selectable even when clipboard access is blocked.

# Same dataset and scaling as the retained SVM script above.
# Compare each (kernel, C) with all other settings held fixed.
for kernel in ['linear', 'rbf', 'poly']:
    for C in [0.1, 100]:
        model = SVC(kernel=kernel, C=C, gamma='scale', degree=3, coef0=1)
        model.fit(X, y)  # X already standardized in the preceding script
        Z = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).reshape(xx.shape)
        plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
        plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap='bwr')
        plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y, cmap='bwr', edgecolors='k')
        plt.scatter(model.support_vectors_[:, 0], model.support_vectors_[:, 1],
                    s=100, facecolors='none', edgecolors='k')
        plt.title(f'{kernel}, C={C}, support vectors={len(model.support_)}')
        plt.xlabel('Standardized x1'); plt.ylabel('Standardized x2')
plt.show()
Correction noteCurated kernel/C panels use actual standardized fitted SVC models. Their input-space contours do not directly show a nonlinear feature-space margin width. No kernel or C setting is universally best.

Misconceptions and tradeoffs

  • The full margin is twice the one-sided distance. Raw decision scores are not geometric distances unless divided by ‖w‖.
  • All four points in the worked geometry lie on supporting planes. An on-margin point may still have zero dual coefficient in a redundant optimum; solver support_ selects nonzero coefficients.
  • Finite C=100 is a soft-margin model. It is not a true hard-margin constraint.
  • SVC has no boosting-style learning_rate, but its QP is solved numerically and iteratively. It is not an analytic one-step solution; other linear SVM training formulations can use SGD.

Five self-checks

Recall first. Writing is optional; reveals are ungraded.

1. What is the canonical full SVM margin width?

Reveal answer 1

2/‖w‖ between the ±1 supporting planes. Distance from the boundary to either plane is 1/‖w‖.

2. What role do support vectors play?

Reveal answer 2

They have nonzero dual coefficients and determine the kernel expansion of the decision function. They lie on the supporting margin or, in soft-margin fits, can lie within it or be misclassified.

3. What changes when C increases?

Reveal answer 3

Margin violations receive greater penalty relative to norm regularization. This often fits training data more tightly and can increase variance; exact margin and test-error behavior are data dependent.

4. Why is scaling usually recommended before an SVM?

Reveal answer 4

Feature scales affect distances, dot products and regularization. Fit a scaler on training data only and apply it to validation/test data, ideally through a pipeline. Already comparable scales may need no further change.

5. How does the kernel trick make a nonlinear classifier?

Reveal answer 5

K(x,z)=⟨Φ(x),Φ(z)⟩ evaluates feature-space inner products without explicitly building Φ. A hyperplane there can be nonlinear in the original input coordinates.

Revision checklist

Course: Support Vector Machine - Notes.pdf, pp. 4–8, 12–14; SVM_Para_Tuning.md. Reference [8].

Algorithm comparison

Filter by task or family, then compare the split, structure and complexity controls. These are typical formulations, not guarantees of predictive superiority.

No algorithms match both filters. Choose All tasks or All families.

Frequent exam contrasts

  • ID3: gain. C4.5: gain ratio plus safeguards. CART: weighted impurity in two children. CHAID: merging plus adjusted tests.
  • CART regression is piecewise constant; first-order MARS is continuous piecewise linear.
  • Random Forest averages learners built independently; boosting adds sequential loss corrections.
  • C controls SVM violation penalties; γ controls kernel locality; η controls boosting contributions. They are not interchangeable.
